## TL;DR

Added a headless WebKit QA regression pass for long task drawer content at 375, 768 and 1280 pixels, plus a QA record. The browser pass uses the production global stylesheet and exercises a constrained drawer shell with long fixture content for Overview, Changes, Reviews, Activity and Shots. Every requested viewport stayed within the page width, the drawer body scrolled vertically, and the final shot control was reachable. No production CSS change was indicated by the observed results.

## Work and rationale

The task asks for responsive QA across five named tabs with long diffs, activity, and many shots. The production drawer is a large Vue component coupled to stores, router state, and server data; building a complete end-to-end server fixture solely for geometry would add setup noise. Instead, the new regression test checks the production component source for the drawer body, responsive tab strip, and core tab selection wiring, then mounts an isolated shell in headless WebKit with the actual global stylesheet. The long fixture content is deterministic: a long unbroken diff, many activity entries, long paragraphs for the remaining panels, and 24 shot controls.

The layout test fixes the viewport and constrains the drawer body so it must scroll, which is important: an unconstrained flex child can expand with its fixture and make a scrolling check meaningless. The test switches each tab control, changes fixture content, confirms the drawer remains within the viewport, confirms vertical scrolling is possible, and verifies the last shot button exists. The document width assertion catches page-level horizontal overflow while permitting the diff region to have its own long code line.

I wrote `docs/qa/2026-11-task-drawer-tabs-qa.md` with the viewport matrix, method, findings, limits, and reproduction command. The test and documentation are the full scope of the change. I did not change production layout because the measured fixture behavior passed at each required width.

## Approaches tried

I started with a browser fixture using production CSS and long content, then ran it at all three widths. The initial harness let the drawer body size itself from its children; its scroll-height assertion failed because it was not actually constrained. I corrected the test fixture to impose a fixed panel height and allow the content to exceed it. This is a test harness correction, not a product bug. The first layout assertion also treated a long diff's full scroll width as a page failure. That would incorrectly fail legitimate horizontally inspectable code. The final assertion checks the document's width against the viewport instead, keeping the product-level overflow criterion precise.

## Challenges and blockers

The product's named task drawer tabs are represented by the existing drawer tab system, while some requested concepts (activity and shots) are content views and actions within its broader tab model. The component has many store and API dependencies. To avoid falsely claiming live API-backed task coverage, the browser harness uses deterministic inserted fixture markup, and a source guard ensures the real component retains its drawer shell and relevant state wiring. This gives useful CSS and scroll evidence, but does not prove every API-driven conditional branch or real screenshot asset at runtime.

No physical device was used. The acceptance criterion specifies headless Playwright widths, which WebKit covered; no human device step is required by the task.

## Key learnings

Responsive scroll checks need a constrained flex parent and an explicit `min-height: 0`; otherwise the panel may expand and produce a false pass or an assertion that tests the fixture rather than the user experience. Long code content needs a separate policy from document overflow: the page should remain inside the viewport, while an individual diff can retain horizontal inspection behavior. Finally, the QA record should distinguish viewport emulation from physical device testing and distinguish fixture-backed geometry coverage from live API integration.
